title: 2 Chronicles 4:11–22
context: This unit summarizes the bronze work of Huram (4:11–18) and then lists the gold furnishings Solomon made for the inside of the house (4:19–22). The parallel is 1 Kings 7:40–50, where the craftsman is named Hiram; Chronicles uses Huram and, in 4:16, Huram-abi, the name given at 2 Chronicles 2:13. Differences are named rather than harmonized: 2 Chronicles 4:17 names the casting site as between Succoth and Zeredah, where 1 Kings 7:46 has Zarethan; and 2 Chronicles 4:19 speaks of the tables with the show bread on them, where 1 Kings 7:48 has the table in the singular, as already noted at 4:8. The pomegranate total in 4:13 matches 1 Kings 7:42. Both traditions read this unit as the formal completion of the furnishing account: the house is equipped, and its meaning will depend on the LORD’s coming to dwell there, which chapter 5 narrates.

verses.text: Huram made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Huram finished doing the work that he did for King Solomon in God’s house:
verses.arminianNotes: Huram makes the pots, shovels, and basins and finishes the work he did for King Solomon in God’s house, as in 1 Kings 7:40. Arminian readers note the faithful completion of a large and demanding commission, and they see the narrator honoring a skilled worker from Tyre who carried his task through to the end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the completion as part of God’s faithfulness in bringing the promised house to completion through human means (2 Samuel 7:13). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as marking the end of Huram’s work and affirm that God is honored through faithful, skilled labor offered for his house.

verses.text: the two pillars, the bowls, the two capitals which were on the top of the pillars, the two networks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the top of the pillars,
verses.arminianNotes: The summary list begins with the two pillars, their bowls and capitals, and the networks that covered them. Arminian readers see the Chronicler recapping the major bronze works of chapter 3 so that the reader can take in the whole, and the repetition serves as a record of completed work rather than new detail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the inventory as a formal summary, much like the closing inventories of the tabernacle in Exodus. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as recapitulation of Huram’s work on the pillars and agree that it raises no theological difference between them, only the honor of finished work.

verses.text: and the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks—two rows of pomegranates for each network, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars.
verses.arminianNotes: The four hundred pomegranates for the two networks are listed, in two rows for each network, matching the total in 1 Kings 7:42. Arminian readers read the count as part of a careful inventory and see no need to build meaning on the number, receiving it as faithful record of decoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also read the verse as part of the summary inventory and note its agreement with the parallel in Kings. Shared ground: both traditions read the pomegranates as recapping the decoration of the capitals, and both decline to construct doctrine from the figure or from the ornament’s design.

verses.text: He also made the bases, and he made the basins on the bases—
verses.arminianNotes: Huram also makes the bases and the basins on them. Chronicles mentions the bases only briefly, without the detailed description found in 1 Kings 7:27–37. Arminian readers see the Chronicler assuming the reader’s knowledge of the fuller account and moving quickly toward the dedication of the house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that Chronicles names the bases without describing them and read the summary as selective rather than contradictory. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the inventory of bronze work and do not treat the brevity of the account as raising any theological question.

verses.text: one sea, and the twelve oxen under it.
verses.arminianNotes: The list continues with the one sea and the twelve oxen under it. Arminian readers see the brief line recalling the great basin already described in 4:2–5, so that the summary gathers each of the major bronze works into one complete record of what Huram made for the LORD’s service.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse as a summary line matching 1 Kings 7:44. Shared ground: both traditions treat the sea as part of the provision for priestly washing named in 4:6, and both read this verse as recapitulation rather than a new point of doctrine or a place for symbolic speculation.

verses.text: Huram-abi also made the pots, the shovels, the forks, and all its vessels for King Solomon, for the LORD’s house, of bright bronze.
verses.arminianNotes: Huram-abi makes the pots, shovels, forks, and other vessels of bright bronze for the LORD’s house. Arminian readers note the craftsman’s full name, given at 2 Chronicles 2:13, and see the Chronicler honoring the skill God supplied through a worker of mixed descent from Dan and Tyre (2 Chronicles 2:14).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the same verse God’s provision of gifted workers for his house, much as he provided Bezalel and Oholiab for the tabernacle (Exodus 31:1–6). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as closing the bronze inventory and affirm that skilled labor offered to God is a real form of service.

verses.text: The king cast them in the plain of the Jordan, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah.
verses.arminianNotes: The king casts the bronze in the clay ground of the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zeredah, where 1 Kings 7:46 has Zarethan. Arminian readers note the difference without resolving it and read the verse as a practical note about where large castings could be made in suitable ground.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the verse as historical detail and name the parallel difference honestly. The precise location of the site is uncertain. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as anchoring the account in real geography and see no theological question raised by the name of the place.

verses.text: Thus Solomon made all these vessels in great abundance, so that the weight of the bronze could not be determined.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon makes the vessels in great abundance, so that the weight of the bronze could not be determined, as 1 Kings 7:47 also says. Arminian readers see the generosity and scale of what was devoted to the LORD’s house, gathered in part from David’s victories (1 Chronicles 18:8).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same abundance as a sign of God’s blessing on David and Solomon, supplying more than could be measured. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing lavish provision for worship, and both may note that the bronze was later carried away to Babylon (2 Kings 25:13–16).

verses.text: Solomon made all the vessels that were in God’s house: the golden altar, the tables with the show bread on them,
verses.arminianNotes: The gold furnishings begin with the golden altar and the tables with the show bread on them. Arminian readers see the inner furnishings as the setting for daily worship before God, with the incense altar and the bread of the presence carried over from the tabernacle into the permanent house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see continuity with the tabernacle furnishings and note the plural tables, where 1 Kings 7:48 has the singular, without harmonizing the two. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing the ordered worship God appointed inside his house, with nothing at stake between them.

verses.text: and the lamp stands with their lamps to burn according to the ordinance before the inner sanctuary, of pure gold;
verses.arminianNotes: The lamp stands with their lamps burn according to the ordinance before the inner sanctuary, all of pure gold. Arminian readers note again that the lights are tended “according to the ordinance” and they see worship shaped by God’s instruction rather than by human invention or preference.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the lamp stands as part of the worship God commanded, continuing the tabernacle lamp stand and its daily care. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as stressing obedience to God’s ordinance in worship and the costly honor given to the place where he chose to put his name.

verses.text: and the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs of gold that was purest gold;
verses.arminianNotes: The flowers, lamps, and tongs are made of the purest gold. Arminian readers see the repeated emphasis on gold as an expression of devotion: the best materials are given for the LORD’s house, and the inventory honors the generosity of king and people in offering what was most precious.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the purest gold as fitting for the inner furnishings, where the most holy things were kept and tended. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as inventory and avoid assigning symbolic meanings to the individual items beyond the text’s own emphasis on purity and value.

verses.text: and the snuffers, the basins, the spoons, and the fire pans of pure gold. As for the entry of the house, its inner doors for the most holy place and the doors of the main hall of the temple were of gold.
verses.arminianNotes: The snuffers, basins, spoons, and fire pans are of pure gold, and the inner doors and the doors of the main hall are of gold. Arminian readers see the list reaching its close with the entrances to the holy places, finishing the house that will now receive the ark and the LORD’s presence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 1 Kings 7:50 speaks of the hinges of the doors, while this verse speaks of the doors, and they name the difference without forcing agreement. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the end of the furnishing account and as preparation for the dedication that follows in chapter 5.
